passage: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
text:
The selected phrase says the Transformer drops both recurrent and convolutional layers, relying only on attention.

Recurrence means processing a sequence one step at a time, with each step depending on the previous hidden state, as in recurrent neural networks. Convolutions slide a small learned filter across the sequence to combine nearby positions. The paper states that its model avoids both and uses attention mechanisms alone p. 1.

In context, this is the central design choice of the paper. Because nothing has to be computed in strict order, the model can process all positions in parallel, which the authors connect to faster training p. 2.

passage: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples
text:
The passage explains that recurrent models must process a sequence one step at a time, so their computation cannot be spread across the positions of a single training example.

The selected sentence says that because each hidden state h_t depends on the previous one h_{t-1}, the model cannot compute position t until position t-1 is done. This sequential dependence blocks parallel computation within one example. Parallelization here means doing many of those computations at once on hardware such as GPUs. The authors note this matters most for long sequences, since memory limits constrain how many examples can be batched together p. 2.

Here the point motivates the Transformer, which drops recurrence so that all positions can be computed together p. 2. In the paper's terms, sequential operations are the minimum number of steps that must run one after another, and recurrent layers need O(n) of them for a sequence of length n p. 6.

passage: before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized
text:
The passage explains where dropout, a randomised switch-off of some activations during training, is applied to reduce overfitting.

The selected sentence says the dropout is applied to each sub-layer's output before that output is added back to the sub-layer's input and then normalised. This is the residual connection followed by layer normalisation, which the paper describes as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) p. 3. Here x is the input to the sub-layer and Sublayer(x) is the sub-layer's own computation.

Dropout is applied to Sublayer(x) only, so the residual path x passes through unchanged. The paper also applies dropout to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings p. 7, and sets the base model's rate to 0.1 p. 7.

passage: the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions
text:
In convolutional models, the work needed to connect two distant positions grows as the gap between them grows, so long-range links become costly.

The passage notes that in ConvS2S the number of operations grows linearly with distance, and in ByteNet logarithmically. Its point is that such growth makes it harder to learn dependencies between far-apart positions p. 2. Here, "operations" means the sequential computation steps a signal must pass through, and "signals" are the information carried from one token to another.

The Transformer avoids this by making the count constant, at the cost of some resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions p. 2. The image confirms this passage reads as printed.

The stronger reading, that attention weights themselves explain what a model does, has been challenged: Serrano and Smith (2019) found attention only noisily predicts input importance, Jain and Wallace (2019) found attention weights often do not correlate with gradient-based importance measures, and Brunner et al. From general knowledge, attention visualizations remain a common diagnostic in Transformer research, but researchers now usually treat them as one signal among several, alongside gradient-based attribution, probing and intervention methods. The claim has not been overturned, but the field has moved toward cautious use of attention as an explanation.

text:
The claim is that self-attention is computationally faster than recurrence when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d p. 6. The objection: this comparison holds only per layer and in raw operation counts, not in wall-clock time on real hardware.

A careful critic would note that the per-layer complexity comparison is O(n·d) for self-attention against O(n·d²) for recurrence, which the table in the document does not show directly but which underlies the claim. Real speed depends on memory access, kernel efficiency and whether the work parallelizes, and the attention score matrix grows with n², so for long sequences memory cost can dominate even when operation counts favor attention. The document itself concedes that for very long sequences the approach needs restriction to a neighborhood of size r p. 7.

The author's best reply is that the advantage is claimed for sentence-length inputs typical of machine translation, where n is smaller than d, and that the parallelism gain is the main practical benefit p. 6.

Reading "no task-specific tuning" as a strong generalization therefore overstates how transferable the architecture is, since the reported F1 reflects a model adjusted to parsing rather than an untouched translation model.

The author's best reply is that the tuning was deliberately minimal, limited to a few hyperparameters, with the architecture and the rest of the configuration left unchanged from the English-to-German base model p. 9, so the result is still evidence of generalization beyond translation.

passage: Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks
text:
The claim that path length governs learnability of long-range dependencies may be overstated, since shorter paths do not guarantee that a model learns useful long-range relations.

Short paths make signals easier to propagate, but a self-attention layer connects all positions in one step without any mechanism that decides which distant positions matter. Attention weights must still be learned from data, and with unrestricted attention the model may spread weight over many irrelevant tokens. The document's own Table 1 counts path length and sequential operations, not whether attention actually selects the right long-range links, so the path-length argument alone does not establish that dependencies are learned well.

The author's best reply is that the paper argues shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn, and it supports this with the observation that attention heads in the figures do capture distant dependencies such as the verb "making" in Figure 3 p. 13.

question: Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?
text:
The document gives only the first half of this explanation. It says that for large dk the dot products grow large in magnitude, and that this pushes the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients p. 4. Footnote 4 explains why the dot products grow: if the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance dk p. 4. So its typical size scales like √dk, which is why the authors divide by √dk.

The document does not explain why large inputs flatten the softmax's gradient, so what follows is from general knowledge. When one input to a softmax is much larger than the others, the output saturates: nearly all the weight goes to that one entry and the rest are close to zero. The softmax's derivative is built from products of the outputs, such as p(1−p). When p is near 0 or 1, that product is near zero. Gradients flowing back through the attention weights then almost vanish, and learning stalls. Scaling by 1/√dk keeps the variance of the scores near 1, which keeps the softmax in a range where gradients are usable.

passage: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information
question: Why use 8 smaller heads instead of one big attention head?
text:
The paper gives two reasons, one stated directly and one implied by its numbers.

The direct reason is on this page: multi-head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, whereas "with a single attention head, averaging inhibits this" p. 5. A single head produces one weighted average of the values, so everything a position gathers gets blended into one pattern. Separate heads, each with its own learned projections, can look for different things at once. The background section frames this as a remedy for the reduced effective resolution caused by averaging attention-weighted positions p. 2.

The cost is not higher. Each head uses dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64, so the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality p. 5.

The experiments support this. With computation held constant, single-head attention was 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, though too many heads (32) also hurt quality p. 9.

The paper doesn't explain why quality drops with too many heads. From general knowledge, a plausible cause is that each head's keys become too small (16 dimensions) to compute compatibility well, which fits their row (B) observation that shrinking dk hurts.

passage: This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure
question: What is label smoothing, and why would it help BLEU while hurting perplexity?
text:
The document only says a little about this. It states that they used label smoothing with value ϵ_ls = 0.1, citing Szegedy et al. [36], and that it "hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score" p. 8. It doesn't define the technique or explain the mechanism in detail, so what follows is from general knowledge.

Label smoothing changes the training target. Instead of telling the model that the correct next token has probability 1 and every other token has 0, you take a small amount of probability mass (here 0.1) and spread it across the other tokens. The model is therefore never rewarded for becoming fully confident.

Perplexity measures how much probability the model puts on the correct tokens, so a model trained to hold back confidence assigns lower probability to the right answers and scores worse. BLEU, however, only looks at the final translated text, not the probabilities. Discouraging overconfidence tends to act as a regularizer and often gives better-calibrated outputs, which can improve the sequences chosen by beam search. That is why the two metrics can move in opposite directions.

passage: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings
question: If learned embeddings performed the same, why keep the sinusoids?
text:
The document gives one reason: the sinusoidal version "may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." p. 6 A learned embedding table only has entries for positions seen in training, whereas a sinusoid is defined for any position.

The authors also had a second motivation for the sinusoids from the start. They hypothesized the functions would make it easy to attend by relative position, since for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be written as a linear function of PE(pos). p. 6

The evidence for the "nearly identical results" claim is Table 3 row (E), where learned embeddings give 25.7 BLEU and 4.92 perplexity against the base model's 25.8 and 4.92. p. 9

Note that the extrapolation benefit is stated as a possibility ("may"), and the document doesn't test it. So the choice rests on a plausible advantage at no measured cost, not on demonstrated superiority.

passage: beam search with a beam size of
question: What does a beam size of 4 mean in practice?
text:
The document doesn't define beam search or explain what beam size means; it only says the models used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, with these hyperparameters chosen after experimentation on the development set p. 8. The explanation below is from general knowledge.

Because the decoder generates one token at a time, the model has to decide how to search for a good output sequence. Greedy decoding keeps only the single most probable token at each step. Beam search instead keeps the 4 highest-scoring partial output sequences (the "beam") at every step. Each of those 4 is extended by every possible next token, all the candidates are scored by cumulative log-probability, and only the best 4 survive to the next step. This continues until the hypotheses finish, and the best completed one is returned.

A larger beam explores more alternatives at more compute cost. The length penalty α mentioned alongside it adjusts scores so longer outputs are not unfairly disfavored.

For comparison, the parsing experiments used a beam size of 21 p. 10.

question: How does the base model differ from the big model, and what did each cost to train?
text:
Size, training length and dropout differ between the two.

Base model: 6 layers, dmodel = 512, dff = 2048, 8 heads with dk = dv = 64, dropout 0.1, and 65M parameters p. 9. It trained for 100,000 steps at about 0.4 seconds per step, roughly 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs p. 7.

Big model: 6 layers, dmodel = 1024, dff = 4096, 16 heads, dropout 0.3, and 213M parameters p. 9. It trained for 300,000 steps at about 1.0 second per step, which is 3.5 days on the same 8 GPUs p. 7. For English-to-French, the big model used dropout 0.1 instead of 0.3 p. 8.

Cost in FLOPs: Table 2 lists 3.3 · 10 for the base model and 2.3 · 10 for the big model, but the exponents are missing from the printed text p. 8. The paper's method is training time × number of GPUs × sustained per-GPU capacity, with 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100 p. 8. Applying that gives about 3.3 · 10^18 for base and 2.3 · 10^19 for big, so the big model costs roughly 7 times more compute. That is my calculation, not a printed figure.

Quality: English-to-German BLEU is 27.3 for base and 28.4 for big, and English-to-French is 38.1 and 41.8 p. 8. The text of section 6.1 gives the big model's French score as 41.0, which conflicts with the 41.8 in the abstract and table, and the document does not explain the discrepancy p. 8.

question: Which ablation results in Table 3 matter most, and why?
text:
Table 3 is on page 9, and the paper itself singles out a few rows. I'd rank them this way.

Row (A), heads: with computation held constant, single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, but quality also drops with too many heads p. 9. The base choice of 8 heads with dk = 64 scores 25.8 BLEU, against 24.9 for one head p. 9. This is the main evidence for multi-head attention, and it shows a sweet spot rather than "more is better."

Row (B), smaller dk: reducing the key size hurts quality. The authors read this as a sign that "determining compatibility is not easy" and that a more sophisticated function than dot product may help p. 9. It is the one result that points to a possible weakness in the design.

Rows (C) and (D), size and dropout: bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting p. 9. These are expected results, but they justify the big configuration, which reaches 26.4 BLEU on the development set p. 9.

Row (E), positional encoding: learned embeddings give 25.7 BLEU against 25.8 for sinusoids, nearly identical p. 9. The authors chose sinusoids because they may extrapolate to longer sequences than seen in training p. 6. Table 3 does not test that claim.

Some row labels in the table, such as which values changed in rows (B) and (C), are missing from the printed text, so for those rows I'm relying on the paper's own description.

Before you start
×

The paper proposes the Transformer, a translation architecture built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It matters because it aims for better quality and far faster parallel training, and the rest of the paper describes, motivates and tests that design.

Key claims

1
The Transformer relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. p. 2
2
Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations, versus O(n) for recurrent layers. p. 6
3
The big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating prior results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. p. 8
4
Ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. p. 9
5
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs well on English constituency parsing, including with only 40K WSJ training sentences. p. 10

Keep in mind

The English-to-French big model score appears as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but as 41.0 in the text of section 6.1. Check which figure you rely on.
Attention itself is not new. The novelty claimed is using it without recurrent or convolutional layers, so read the Background section with that distinction in mind.
Perplexities in Table 3 are per-wordpiece under byte-pair encoding, so they should not be compared with per-word perplexities from other work. Training cost figures are estimates built from GPU time and assumed sustained TFLOPS.
